questions.q: What should your first sentence to the VP of Sales be?
options: A summary of how you built the dashboard
The conclusion: a number, a verdict and a hint of the action
An apology for any data problems
A list of every report you used
questions.explain: Executives want the answer first. Method and detail follow only if the VP asks for them.

questions.q: How many findings should the core of the presentation contain?
options: One per dashboard component
None; only a recommendation
As many as fit on the dashboard
About three, ranked by importance
questions.explain: Three ranked findings are memorable. The rest of the dashboard stays available as backup if asked.

questions.q: The VP says the win rate looks low. What is the best response?
options: Say you will fix the dashboard later without explanation
Insist the number is correct and move on
Explain it is measured by count, and offer to add a by-amount view
Change the number in the meeting
questions.explain: State the definition, then offer to show a different cut. Defining the metric clearly turns an objection into a useful discussion.

questions.q: You are asked for a regional breakdown that the dashboard does not include. What should you do?
options: Estimate a plausible split on the spot
Ignore the question
Say it is not in this version, note it, and give a follow-up date
Blame the data
questions.explain: Never invent a figure in the room. Acknowledge the gap, record it, and commit to a date.

options: It lists several equally weighted options
It is one specific action with an owner and a date
It avoids mentioning numbers
It waits until the next quarter
questions.explain: One specific action with an owner and a date is easy to approve and easy to check. Extra ideas can be mentioned as follow-ups.
